characters: Delanyo: an inquisitive eight-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a sky-blue collared school shirt, khaki shorts, and brown sandals.
Tiwaa: his bright eight-year-old Ghanaian female classmate with neat braided plaits and yellow hair beads, wearing a matching sky-blue-and-khaki school dress.
Their teacher: a warm Ghanaian woman wearing an indigo-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious boy’s voice for Delanyo; a bright girl’s voice for Tiwaa
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and clear, with a pause at each test (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, drippy xylophone that fades like mist (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Puddles after the rains and wet clothes drying on a line are everyday sights across Ghana. The story links them with the water cycle that children meet in Integrated Science.
The story is accurate that some rainwater also sinks into the ground rather than claiming the sun took every drop.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that the explanation of evaporation matches the Integrated Science syllabus and that water vapour is described accurately as an invisible gas.
Confirm that the two-saucer test works clearly within two hours on a sunny day.

teacherGuide.overview: A two-saucer investigation showing that water evaporates faster in the sun than in the shade. Learners keep the test fair (equal water and matching saucers) and connect evaporation to drying clothes, clouds, and rain.
learningGoals: Carry out a fair two-saucer comparison.
Connect evaporation to drying clothes, clouds, and rain.
beforeReading: Ask: where does the water in a schoolyard puddle go when the sun comes out?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and ask: why must both saucers hold the exact same amount of water?
afterReading: Set up the two-saucer test, mark the starting water rim with a pencil, and compare after two hours.
Hang one damp cloth in the sun and an identical damp cloth in the shade and compare how fast they dry.
discussion: Why did the water level drop faster in the sunny saucer?
Where does the invisible water vapour go?
reflection: Where else at home or school have you noticed water drying up?

support: Use two clear cups and draw the before-and-after water heights side by side.
stretch: Predict what would happen on a cool, cloudy morning and test your prediction.

culturalNotes: Puddles after the rains and wet clothes drying on a line are everyday sights across Ghana. The story links them with the water cycle that children meet in Integrated Science.
The story is accurate that some rainwater also sinks into the ground rather than claiming the sun took every drop.
localiseThis: Connect the lesson to rainy-season puddles and household washing lines.
Use cool tap water only; never use hot water with young learners.

factCheck.claim: Sunlight warms liquid water so it evaporates faster into invisible water vapour in the air.
factCheck.explanation: Solar warmth gives surface water molecules enough energy to escape as invisible water vapour gas; higher up, cooling vapour condenses into cloud droplets.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Ghana Primary Integrated Science Curriculum (Water Cycle and Evaporation)
